content: A hybrid open access journal is a type of academic journal where only a subset of the articles are made freely accessible to the public. Authors who wish to make their articles open access are typically required to pay a publication fee, also referred to as a processing fee, to the publisher. The term Hybrid Open Access Journal is the most commonly used designation for this model, though other terms such as OA by the Article and Optional OA have also been employed. Additionally, Open Choice is sometimes used generically, though it specifically refers to a scheme by Springer. The model has also been referred to as the Walker-Prosser model, named after its originators. It is important to note that the definition of open access can vary among publishers. True open access involves not only free access to content but also minimal permission barriers. For instance, Creative Commons licenses offer varying levels of openness, with the most restrictive license allowing users to download and share works as long as proper attribution is given, the original work is linked, and the content is neither altered nor used for commercial purposes. Other licenses are more permissive. The concept of hybrid open access was first proposed several years ago. Thomas J. Walker initially suggested that authors could pay a fee to increase the visibility of their work. The first journal to adopt this model was Walker's own Florida Journal of Entomology, which later extended the approach to other publications of the Entomological Society of America. David Prosser refined the idea in 2003 in the journal Learned Publishing. Each publisher offering a hybrid open access model uses a unique name for their program. For example: AlphaMed Press refers to it as the Open Access Option. The American Chemical Society calls it Author Choice. Elsevier uses the term Sponsored Article. Springer refers to it as Open Choice. Oxford University Press calls it Oxford Open. Many other publishers have their own branded names for similar programs. One of the proposed effects of hybrid open access on subscription prices is the potential for a reduction in library subscription costs. Since library budgets are often a source of funding for open access fees, it is argued that the cost of subscriptions should decrease proportionally as more articles are funded through author payments. Springer’s Open Choice program was the first to implement a mechanism to reduce subscription prices based on the proportion of author-funded articles. This approach has since been adopted, with variations, by other publishers. However, the impact of these fees on subscription pricing is often delayed, with changes typically reflected two years after the fees are paid. For publishers, hybrid open access offers a way to mitigate the financial risks associated with fully open access journals. In a fully open access model, publishers must rely entirely on author-side fees, which can be uncertain, especially during the initial stages of a journal's launch. In contrast, hybrid journals maintain a dual revenue stream: subscription income and fees from authors who opt for open access. This model allows publishers to provide open access only for articles where payment is made, ensuring financial stability regardless of the success of the open access component. For authors, hybrid open access expands the range of publication options. Instead of being limited to fully open access journals, authors can choose from a broader selection of hybrid journals, including those published by major academic publishers. However, authors must still secure funding to cover the publication fees. Many funding agencies allow authors to use grant funds or apply for supplementary funding to pay these fees. While only a minority of fully open access journals charge publication fees, nearly all hybrid journals do. Funding agencies that support open access fees generally do not differentiate between fully open access and hybrid journals. Some variations of the hybrid model exist. For example, the American Society of Plant Biologists (ASPB) has implemented a unique policy for its journal Plant Physiology. Articles contributed by society members are made open access immediately upon publication at no additional cost. Non-member authors can achieve open access by paying a fee of $1,000. However, since ASPB membership costs only $115 per year, this initiative is expected to encourage more authors to join the society.
